topic: how animals get ready for winter
why: Following how frogs, chipmunks, bees, voles and hares get through winter helps your child explain how a body or a home can hold on to heat or survive the cold.
teaser: Meet a frog that freezes, a chipmunk that cools down, bees that shiver and voles that live under the snow.
title: How Animals Get Ready for Winter
question: How do animals stay alive through a cold winter?
idea: Animals use different plans for winter: some hide food, some survive freezing with sugar or glycerol, some let their bodies cool down to save energy, some make heat by shivering, and some live under a snow blanket.

curiosity.intro: Start with one cold woods. Find the animals that stay, and look at the plan each one uses.
curiosity.carryForward: Look for the plan: hide food, freeze safely, cool down, make heat, or stay under the snow.

questions.question: How can a wood frog freeze and live?
questions.notice: Find the small frog tucked under the fallen leaves, and the fuzzy banded caterpillar resting on a leaf nearby.
questions.say: When a wood frog starts to freeze, its liver pours out a sugar called glucose. Ice forms in its body, but outside its cells, and the glucose helps protect the cells. When the frog thaws, its heart is the first part to start again.
questions.try: Draw a big circle for one frog cell. Draw ice crystals only outside the circle. Draw sugar dots near the cell. Tell how the sugar helps keep the cell safe while ice forms around it.

questions.question: How does a chipmunk save energy all winter?
questions.notice: Find the chipmunk curled up tight in a nest of leaves under the snowy ground.
questions.say: A chipmunk is a small hibernator. Its body gets much colder on purpose. This is called torpor, and it saves energy. For most small hibernators like this one, hibernation is many long torpor stretches in a row, with short warm-ups between them. To help warm back up, many mammal hibernators burn a special fat called brown fat.
questions.try: Sit very still and count your breaths for 30 seconds. Then march in place for 30 seconds and count again. Tell which time used more energy. In torpor, an animal slows its body way down to save energy.

questions.question: How do honeybees stay warm without hibernating?
questions.notice: Look at the round ball of bees on the comb. Find the bees on the outside and the bees packed in the middle.
questions.say: Honeybees do not hibernate. They pack into a ball called a winter cluster. The outside bees make a blanket. The inside bees shiver their flight muscles without moving their wings, which makes heat. When there are no baby bees in the hive, the middle of the cluster is kept above about 64 degrees Fahrenheit.
questions.try: Fill two jars with warm tap water and close the lids. Wrap one jar in a thick towel or some socks, like the outside bees. Leave the other jar bare. Wait 20 minutes, then touch both jars and tell which one stayed warmer.

questions.question: Why can a mouse stay warmer under the snow?
questions.notice: Find the tunnel along the ground under the snow, the mouse inside it, and the small hole that reaches up to the air.
questions.say: The space between the ground and the snow is called the subnivean zone. About six inches of snow works like a blanket, so this space stays near 32 degrees Fahrenheit even when the air above is much colder. Voles and mice tunnel and eat there, and small air holes let carbon dioxide out.
questions.try: Put two kitchen thermometers in the freezer. Bury one in a thick pile of cotton balls, like a snow blanket. Leave the other one bare. After 20 minutes, read both and tell which one is warmer.

plates.title: A cold woods
plates.alt: Big and Little Wonderer stand at the edge of a quiet late-fall woods with a light dusting of snow, watching a small chickadee tuck a seed into the bark of a tree.
plates.caption: Winter is coming. Every animal here needs a plan.

plates.title: Freeze and wait
plates.alt: A small brown wood frog rests under a layer of fallen leaves on the forest floor, with a fuzzy black-and-brown woolly bear caterpillar resting on a leaf nearby.
plates.caption: A wood frog and a woolly bear can both freeze and live.

plates.title: Cool and slow
plates.alt: A cutaway of the ground shows a chipmunk curled into a tight ball in a leaf nest under the snowy ground.
plates.caption: A chipmunk saves energy by letting its body cool down.

plates.title: Shiver and huddle
plates.alt: A cutaway of a wooden beehive shows honeybees packed into one round ball on the honeycomb.
plates.caption: Honeybees huddle in a ball and shiver to make heat.

plates.title: Under the snow
plates.alt: Big and Little Wonderer kneel on a snowy meadow beside a small air hole, above a cutaway showing a small mouse in a tunnel along the ground beneath the snow.
plates.caption: The space under a thick snow blanket stays near freezing, not far below it.

plates.title: A white coat
plates.alt: A white snowshoe hare sits on brown fallen leaves at the edge of a woods, with only small patches of snow around it.
plates.caption: A hare's coat may turn white before the snow comes.

reading.title: Six winter plans
reading.coverText: Follow the animals of one cold woods and the plan each one uses to get through winter.
reading.parentNote: Age 8. Welcome spoken answers, pointing, drawing, and dictation; the plates show the ideas rather than exact measurements.
reading.foldableTitle: A little book of winter plans
reading.foldableNote: Carry six winter plans in a small book.

beats.title: A cold woods
beats.passage: Big and Little walked to the edge of the woods. The days were getting short. A chickadee tucked a seed into a crack in the bark, then flew to another tree. Big said chickadees hide food in many spots in fall. They use a part of the brain called the hippocampus to find those spots again later.
beats.prompt: Why might a chickadee hide its seeds in many different places?

foldable.heading: A cold woods
foldable.body: A chickadee hides seeds in many spots in fall. It uses a brain part called the hippocampus to find them again.

beats.title: Freeze and wait
beats.passage: Under the leaves, a wood frog freezes. Ice forms in its body, but outside its cells. Its liver pours out glucose, a kind of sugar, that helps protect the cells. A woolly bear caterpillar makes glycerol, an antifreeze-like protectant. In a lab test, caterpillars cooled slowly for weeks moved again after a week frozen at about -4 degrees Fahrenheit.
beats.prompt: What does the sugar do for a wood frog as it freezes?

foldable.heading: Freeze and wait
foldable.body: A wood frog freezes, but the ice stays outside its cells. Sugar from its liver helps keep the cells safe.

beats.title: Cool and slow
beats.passage: In winter, a chipmunk's body gets much colder on purpose. This is called torpor, and it saves energy. For most small hibernators, hibernation is many long torpor stretches with short warm-ups between them. Many mammal hibernators burn brown fat, a special fat that makes heat, to warm back up. A bear is different. It cools only a few degrees.
beats.prompt: How does getting colder help a chipmunk save energy?

foldable.heading: Cool and slow
foldable.body: A chipmunk lets its body get cold to save energy. Many mammal hibernators burn brown fat to warm up.

beats.title: Shiver and huddle
beats.passage: Honeybees do not hibernate. In winter they pack together into one ball called a cluster. The bees on the outside make a living blanket. The bees in the middle shiver their flight muscles without moving their wings. That shivering makes heat. When there are no baby bees, the middle stays warmer than about 64 degrees Fahrenheit.
beats.prompt: Why do the outside bees and the inside bees have different jobs?

foldable.heading: Shiver and huddle
foldable.body: Bees pack into a ball. Outside bees make a blanket. Inside bees shiver their flight muscles to make heat.

beats.title: Under the snow
beats.passage: Little found a tiny hole in the snow. Big said it was an air hole. Under the snow, voles and mice dig tunnels along the ground. This space is called the subnivean zone. About six inches of snow works like a blanket, so it stays near 32 degrees Fahrenheit there, even when the air above is much colder. The air holes let carbon dioxide out.
beats.prompt: Why is it warmer under the snow than in the air above it?

foldable.heading: Under the snow
foldable.body: Under the snow, mice tunnel and eat. A thick snow blanket keeps their space near freezing, not far below it.

beats.title: A white coat
beats.passage: In snowy places, most snowshoe hares grow a white coat in fall. In one study, the change started on about the same dates every year, snow or no snow. Scientists think the length of the day is the main trigger. The change takes about 40 days. So when snow comes late, a white hare can end up sitting on brown leaves.
beats.prompt: Why might a white hare be easy to spot when snow comes late?

foldable.heading: A white coat
foldable.body: In snowy places, most snowshoe hares turn white in fall. Scientists think day length starts it, even if snow is late.

math.title: Winter groups and arrays
math.intro: Use repeated addition to count equal groups and rows. These numbers are for a math story.

tasks.prompt: A chickadee hides 4 seeds in each of 3 trees. How many seeds does it hide altogether?
tasks.label: TASK 1

tasks.prompt: Little lines up pinecones in 2 rows with 5 pinecones in each row. How many pinecones are there altogether?
tasks.label: TASK 2

tasks.prompt: Big draws 4 sleeping chipmunks with 4 leaves on each one. How many leaves is that altogether?
tasks.label: TASK 3

tasks.prompt: Big draws bees on a cluster in 5 rows with 5 bees in each row. How many bees are drawn altogether?
tasks.label: TASK 4

tasks.prompt: There are 4 vole tunnels under the snow, and each tunnel has 2 air holes. How many air holes are there altogether?
tasks.label: TASK 5

tasks.prompt: Little finds hare tracks in 3 rows with 5 tracks in each row. How many tracks are there altogether?
tasks.label: TASK 6

math.extension: Choose one problem and draw it as rows of dots. Count the dots to check.
math.printNote: Show your thinking with numbers, marks, or words.
math.parentNote: Six equal-group and array problems use rows and columns from 2 to 5 and repeated addition. The numbers are for practice, not real animal counts.
math.answerKeyIntro: Add the same number once for each group or row. Welcome a drawing of dots as an explanation.

writing.intro: Choose one animal. Say your idea first, then draw or write it.
writing.draw: Draw one animal in its winter place and show how it stays alive.

answers.label: Reading · 1
answers.text: Ice forms in the frog's body but outside its cells, and glucose (sugar) from its liver helps protect the cells. When it thaws, its heart starts first.

answers.label: Reading · 2
answers.text: A chipmunk saves energy by letting its body get cold in torpor, with short warm-ups; many mammal hibernators use brown fat to warm back up. Honeybees do not hibernate: they huddle in a cluster and the inside bees shiver their flight muscles.

answers.label: Reading · 3
answers.text: About six inches of snow works like a blanket, so the space under it stays near 32 degrees Fahrenheit. Scientists think day length starts a hare's coat change, so if snow comes late, a white hare can sit on brown leaves.

answers.label: Writing
answers.text: Accept a spoken, dictated, drawn, or written sentence that tells how one animal gets through winter.

parentGuidance: Wood frogs: ice forms outside cells while liver glucose protects them; on thawing the heart returns first. Chickadees cache food and use the hippocampus to find it; one study found more new neurons there in fall, but later studies disagree and the cells seem to replace old ones, so we never say they grow bigger brains. In most small mammal hibernators, hibernation is long torpor bouts with brief rewarming, often fuelled by brown fat; a bear cools only a few degrees. With no brood, honeybee clusters keep the core above about 64 F. Day length is thought to trigger the hare molt (about 40 days). About 6 in of snow keeps the subnivean zone near 32 F. Woolly bears make glycerol; we skip the stripe folklore. Watch wildlife from a distance; use warm, not hot, water.

questions.answer: Glucose, a sugar from the frog's liver, helps protect its cells while ice forms outside them.

questions.prompt: Why does a chipmunk cool down?
questions.answer: In torpor its body gets colder and slower, which saves energy.

questions.prompt: How do inside bees make heat?
questions.answer: The inside bees shiver their flight muscles without moving their wings.

questions.prompt: Why is it warmer under snow?
questions.answer: About six inches of snow insulates the space, so it stays near 32 degrees Fahrenheit.
